title: Sum of Unique Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of values that appear exactly once.
Idea: `sumOfUnique` uses `Counter(nums)` in Python and a `HashMap<Integer,Integer>` named `c` in Java; it adds each value whose frequency is exactly one.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counts identify singleton values, and the second pass sums only those values.
Invariant: The frequency table records the count of every value; the final sum includes only values with count one.
Edge cases: Repeated values contribute nothing even if they appear twice; negative values are valid; the Java second pass over `nums` still adds a unique value only once.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the frequency map.
complexity_reason: Frequency counts identify singleton values, and the second pass sums only those values.

title: Sum of Unique Elements
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of values that appear exactly once.
Idea: `sumOfUnique` uses `Counter(nums)` in Python and a `HashMap<Integer,Integer>` named `c` in Java; it adds each value whose frequency is exactly one.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counts identify singleton values, and the second pass sums only those values.
Invariant: The frequency table records the count of every value; the final sum includes only values with count one.
Edge cases: Repeated values contribute nothing even if they appear twice; negative values are valid; the Java second pass over `nums` still adds a unique value only once.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the frequency map.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int sumOfUnique(int[] nums){Map<Integer,Integer>c=new HashMap<>();for(int x:nums)c.put(x,c.getOrDefault(x,0)+1);int s=0;for(int x:nums)if(c.get(x)==1)s+=x;return s;} }
complexity_reason: Frequency counts identify singleton values, and the second pass sums only those values.

title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the array is non-decreasing after some rotation.
Idea: `check` counts circular drops using `nums[i] > nums[(i+1)%len(nums)]`; Java increments `drops` and exits once a second drop appears.
Technique and why it applies: Checking each adjacent pair including the wraparound detects whether one rotation can make the array sorted.
Invariant: A nondecreasing array under rotation has at most one strict descent when the last element is compared back to the first.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values are allowed; the wraparound pair is essential; the problem supplies a non-empty array for modulo indexing.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Checking each adjacent pair including the wraparound detects whether one rotation can make the array sorted.

title: Check if Array Is Sorted and Rotated
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the array is non-decreasing after some rotation.
Idea: `check` counts circular drops using `nums[i] > nums[(i+1)%len(nums)]`; Java increments `drops` and exits once a second drop appears.
Technique and why it applies: Checking each adjacent pair including the wraparound detects whether one rotation can make the array sorted.
Invariant: A nondecreasing array under rotation has at most one strict descent when the last element is compared back to the first.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values are allowed; the wraparound pair is essential; the problem supplies a non-empty array for modulo indexing.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public boolean check(int[] nums){int drops=0;for(int i=0;i<nums.length;i++)if(nums[i]>nums[(i+1)%nums.length]&&++drops>1)return false;return true;} }
complexity_reason: Checking each adjacent pair including the wraparound detects whether one rotation can make the array sorted.

title: Merge Strings Alternately
notes:
Task and constraints: Merge two strings by alternating characters, appending any remaining suffix.
Idea: `mergeAlternately` appends `word1[i]` and `word2[i]` while both indices exist, then appends whichever suffix remains.
Technique and why it applies: Appending paired characters and then the unconsumed suffix produces the required merge in linear time.
Invariant: The output preserves each input's character order and alternates characters until one string is exhausted.
Edge cases: Inputs may have unequal lengths; the leftover suffix must not be dropped; empty strings are handled by the remaining-suffix logic.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) output space.
complexity_reason: Appending paired characters and then the unconsumed suffix produces the required merge in linear time.

Edge cases: Inputs may have unequal lengths; the leftover suffix must not be dropped; empty strings are handled by the remaining-suffix logic.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) output space.
code: class Solution { public String mergeAlternately(String word1,String word2){StringBuilder b=new StringBuilder();for(int i=0;i<Math.max(word1.length(),word2.length());i++){if(i<word1.length())b.append(word1.charAt(i));if(i<word2.length())b.append(word2.charAt(i));}return b.toString();} }
complexity_reason: Appending paired characters and then the unconsumed suffix produces the required merge in linear time.

title: Count Items Matching a Rule
approach_name: Map rule key to field index
notes:
Task and constraints: Count items whose selected type, color, or name equals the requested rule value.
Idea: `countMatches` maps `ruleKey` to item field index 0, 1, or 2, then counts rows whose selected field equals `ruleValue`.
Technique and why it applies: Mapping the rule key to a field index lets one loop handle all three matching rules.
Invariant: The chosen index consistently selects type, color, or name from each three-field item.
Edge cases: Only the requested field is compared; unknown rule keys are excluded by the problem constraints; all items are checked once.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Mapping the rule key to a field index lets one loop handle all three matching rules.

Technique and why it applies: Mapping the rule key to a field index lets one loop handle all three matching rules.
Invariant: The chosen index consistently selects type, color, or name from each three-field item.
Edge cases: Only the requested field is compared; unknown rule keys are excluded by the problem constraints; all items are checked once.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int countMatches(List<List<String>> items,String ruleKey,String ruleValue){int idx=ruleKey.equals("type")?0:ruleKey.equals("color")?1:2,ans=0;for(List<String>it:items)if(it.get(idx).equals(ruleValue))ans++;return ans;} }
complexity_reason: Mapping the rule key to a field index lets one loop handle all three matching rules.

title: Find Nearest Point That Has Same X or Y Coordinate
approach_name: Minimum Manhattan distance among valid points
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the earliest index of a point sharing x or y with the query and having minimum Manhattan distance, or -1.
Idea: `nearestValidPoint` scans points in index order, filters for matching x or y, computes Manhattan distance, and updates the best candidate only when the distance is strictly smaller.
Technique and why it applies: Filtering eligible points and updating only on a strictly smaller distance preserves the earliest tie.
Invariant: `best` remains the smallest distance among eligible points seen so far; strict improvement preserves the earliest index on ties.
Edge cases: Points sharing neither coordinate are ignored; if none qualify return -1; equal-distance ties keep the earlier point.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Filtering eligible points and updating only on a strictly smaller distance preserves the earliest tie.

title: Find Nearest Point That Has Same X or Y Coordinate
approach_name: Minimum Manhattan distance among valid points
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the earliest index of a point sharing x or y with the query and having minimum Manhattan distance, or -1.
Idea: `nearestValidPoint` scans points in index order, filters for matching x or y, computes Manhattan distance, and updates the best candidate only when the distance is strictly smaller.
Technique and why it applies: Filtering eligible points and updating only on a strictly smaller distance preserves the earliest tie.
Invariant: `best` remains the smallest distance among eligible points seen so far; strict improvement preserves the earliest index on ties.
Edge cases: Points sharing neither coordinate are ignored; if none qualify return -1; equal-distance ties keep the earlier point.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int nearestValidPoint(int x,int y,int[][] points){int best=-1,dist=Integer.MAX_VALUE;for(int i=0;i<points.length;i++){int a=points[i][0],b=points[i][1];if(a==x||b==y){int d=Math.abs(a-x)+Math.abs(b-y);if(d<dist){dist=d;best=i;}}}return best;} }
complexity_reason: Filtering eligible points and updating only on a strictly smaller distance preserves the earliest tie.

title: Determine Color of a Chessboard Square
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the named chessboard square is white.
Idea: `squareIsWhite` converts the file letter to a zero-based column and combines its parity with the row digit's parity.
Technique and why it applies: Coordinate parity identifies the square color without constructing a chessboard.
Invariant: Adjacent squares have opposite color, so the parity of the row and column coordinates determines the color.
Edge cases: Files range from a through h and ranks from 1 through 8; input is a valid square name.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space.
code:
class Solution:
 def squareIsWhite(self,coordinates):return (ord(coordinates[0])-ord('a')+int(coordinates[1]))%2==0
complexity_reason: Coordinate parity identifies the square color without constructing a chessboard.

code: class Solution { public boolean squareIsWhite(String coordinates){return ((coordinates.charAt(0)-'a'+coordinates.charAt(1)-'0')%2)==0;} }

title: Sign of the Product of an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return 0 if any value is zero, otherwise return the sign based on the count of negative values.
Idea: `arraySign` returns zero immediately on any zero; otherwise it toggles or counts negative values and returns -1 for odd parity and 1 for even parity.
Technique and why it applies: Counting negative parity avoids multiplying values and prevents overflow while determining the product sign.
Invariant: The product sign depends only on whether any factor is zero and the parity of negative factors, not their magnitudes.
Edge cases: Negative values with odd count produce -1; an empty product is not part of the usual constraints; large products are never computed.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Counting negative parity avoids multiplying values and prevents overflow while determining the product sign.

title: Sign of the Product of an Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return 0 if any value is zero, otherwise return the sign based on the count of negative values.
Idea: `arraySign` returns zero immediately on any zero; otherwise it toggles or counts negative values and returns -1 for odd parity and 1 for even parity.
Technique and why it applies: Counting negative parity avoids multiplying values and prevents overflow while determining the product sign.
Invariant: The product sign depends only on whether any factor is zero and the parity of negative factors, not their magnitudes.
Edge cases: Negative values with odd count produce -1; an empty product is not part of the usual constraints; large products are never computed.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public int arraySign(int[] nums){int neg=0;for(int x:nums){if(x==0)return 0;if(x<0)neg++;}return neg%2==0?1:-1;} }
complexity_reason: Counting negative parity avoids multiplying values and prevents overflow while determining the product sign.

title: Check if the Sentence Is Pangram
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the sentence contains every lowercase English letter.
Idea: `checkIfPangram` tracks distinct lowercase letters in a set or a 26-slot presence structure and checks whether all 26 appeared.
Technique and why it applies: Tracking distinct letters directly verifies complete alphabet coverage without relying on sentence length.
Invariant: The number of distinct lowercase letters seen increases only on first occurrence, and pangram status requires all 26.
Edge cases: Repeated letters do not increase distinct coverage; the input is lowercase English text; a sentence missing any letter fails.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed 26-letter alphabet.
code:
class Solution:
 def checkIfPangram(self,sentence):return len(set(sentence))==26
complexity_reason: Tracking distinct letters directly verifies complete alphabet coverage without relying on sentence length.

title: Check if the Sentence Is Pangram
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if the sentence contains every lowercase English letter.
Idea: `checkIfPangram` tracks distinct lowercase letters in a set or a 26-slot presence structure and checks whether all 26 appeared.
Technique and why it applies: Tracking distinct letters directly verifies complete alphabet coverage without relying on sentence length.
Invariant: The number of distinct lowercase letters seen increases only on first occurrence, and pangram status requires all 26.
Edge cases: Repeated letters do not increase distinct coverage; the input is lowercase English text; a sentence missing any letter fails.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the fixed 26-letter alphabet.
code: class Solution { public boolean checkIfPangram(String sentence){boolean[]seen=new boolean[26];int n=0;for(char c:sentence.toCharArray())if(!seen[c-'a']){seen[c-'a']=true;n++;}return n==26;} }
complexity_reason: Tracking distinct letters directly verifies complete alphabet coverage without relying on sentence length.

title: Sum of Digits in Base K
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of the base-k digits of n.
Idea: `sumBase` repeatedly adds `n % k` to the total and replaces `n` with integer division `n // k` (or `/=` in Java).
Technique and why it applies: Remainder and integer division extract base-k digits one at a time without string conversion.
Invariant: At each iteration the remainder is the least-significant remaining base-k digit, and division removes that digit.
Edge cases: For n=0 the digit sum is zero; k is at least two; positive n eventually reaches zero.
Complexity: O(log_k n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Remainder and integer division extract base-k digits one at a time without string conversion.

title: Sum of Digits in Base K
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the sum of the base-k digits of n.
Idea: `sumBase` repeatedly adds `n % k` to the total and replaces `n` with integer division `n // k` (or `/=` in Java).
Technique and why it applies: Remainder and integer division extract base-k digits one at a time without string conversion.
Invariant: At each iteration the remainder is the least-significant remaining base-k digit, and division removes that digit.
Edge cases: For n=0 the digit sum is zero; k is at least two; positive n eventually reaches zero.
Complexity: O(log_k n) time and O(1) space.
code: class Solution { public int sumBase(int n,int k){int s=0;while(n>0){s+=n%k;n/=k;}return s;} }
complexity_reason: Remainder and integer division extract base-k digits one at a time without string conversion.

title: Replace All Digits with Characters
approach_name: Shift each preceding character by the digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Replace each digit at an odd index with the previous character shifted forward by that digit.
Idea: `replaceDigits` copies even-index characters and at each odd index shifts the preceding original character forward by the numeric value of the current digit.
Technique and why it applies: Using the preceding character plus the digit offset decodes each encoded position directly.
Invariant: Each digit position is derived from the character immediately before it in the original string, not from a previously shifted result.
Edge cases: The input alternates letters and digits; shifted letters stay within the lowercase alphabet under the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Using the preceding character plus the digit offset decodes each encoded position directly.

title: Replace All Digits with Characters
approach_name: Shift each preceding character by the digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Replace each digit at an odd index with the previous character shifted forward by that digit.
Idea: `replaceDigits` copies even-index characters and at each odd index shifts the preceding original character forward by the numeric value of the current digit.
Technique and why it applies: Using the preceding character plus the digit offset decodes each encoded position directly.
Invariant: Each digit position is derived from the character immediately before it in the original string, not from a previously shifted result.
Edge cases: The input alternates letters and digits; shifted letters stay within the lowercase alphabet under the problem constraints.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public String replaceDigits(String s){char[]a=s.toCharArray();for(int i=1;i<a.length;i+=2)a[i]=(char)(a[i-1]+a[i]-'0');return new String(a);} }
complexity_reason: Using the preceding character plus the digit offset decodes each encoded position directly.
